name: Papiamento
family: Iberian-based (Portuguese and Spanish) creole of the ABC islands, with strong Dutch influence
variety: Papiamentu of Curaçao (the variety of the tone studies), in the phonemic spelling of Curaçao and Bonaire; Aruban Papiamento uses an etymological spelling
sources: Kouwenberg, Silvia and Murray, Eric (1994). Papiamentu. München: Lincom Europa (Languages of the World/Materials 83).
Römer, Raúl G. (1991). Studies in Papiamentu Tonology. Amsterdam and Kingston: Caribbean Culture Studies 5.
Römer, Raúl G. (1977). Polarization phenomena in Papiamentu. Amsterdam Creole Studies 1.
Remijsen, Bert and van Heuven, Vincent J. (2005). Stress, tone and discourse prominence in the Curaçao dialect of Papiamentu. Phonology 22, 205-235.
Rivera-Castillo, Yolanda and Pickering, Lucy (2004). Phonetic correlates of stress and tone in a mixed system. Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages 19(2), 261-284.
Kouwenberg, Silvia (2004). The grammatical function of Papiamentu tone. Journal of Portuguese Linguistics 3(2).

Maurer, Philippe (1998). El papiamentu de Curazao. In Perl and Schwegler (eds.), América negra: panorámica actual de los estudios lingüísticos sobre variedades hispanas, portuguesas y criollas. Frankfurt: Vervuert.
Maurer, Philippe (2013). Papiamentu. In Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath and Huber (eds.), The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages, volume II. Oxford University Press.
contrasts: close-mid versus open-mid vowels, marked in the Curaçao spelling (e versus è, o versus ò)
front rounded vowels /y ø/ (written ü, ù), mostly in words from Dutch (hür 'rent', bùs 'bus', minüt)
lexical stress: penultimate versus final (para [ˈpara] versus pará [paˈra] 'stopped')

lexical tone, independent of stress: words of two syllables with penultimate stress have either a high-low or a low-high pitch pattern (para high-low 'bird' versus para low-high 'to stop'; biaha high-low 'trip' versus biaha low-high 'to travel'; sala high-low 'living room' versus sala low-high 'to salt')
voiced versus voiceless obstruents, including /z v ʒ/ from Dutch and Iberian sources
/x/ (written g before e, i, and in Dutch words) versus /h/
allophony: word-final n is velar [ŋ] and the vowel before it is nasalised (pan [paŋ], bon [boŋ], nan)
schwa [ə] occurs only unstressed, mainly in final -er, -el, -en (hòmber [ˈhɔmbər])
/b d ɡ/ stay stops between vowels; there is no Spanish-type weakening to fricatives
/r/ is an alveolar tap or short trill; some speakers use a uvular r
/ɲ/ (written ñ) and the affricates /tʃ dʒ/ (written ch, dj) are single segments
syllable_structure: (C)(C)(C)V(C)(C); initial s plus consonant clusters are common (skol, stul, sker)
phonotactics: words of Iberian origin have lost the initial vowel before s plus consonant and many final vowels (skol, kas, hòmber)
verbs have no final r (kanta, kome, drumi)
final consonant clusters occur in Dutch loans

stress.rule: Words ending in a vowel are stressed on the penultimate syllable and words ending in a consonant on the last; exceptions carry an acute accent in the Curaçao spelling. Verbs of two syllables have penultimate stress, verbs of three or more syllables and all past participles have final stress (kuminsá, kantá).
stress.cues: duration and intensity carry stress; pitch carries tone (Rivera-Castillo and Pickering 2004; Remijsen and van Heuven 2005)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none, apart from schwa in a few unstressed endings
rhythm.notes: No rhythm measurements for Papiamento are cited here; the class is assumed from the descriptive literature.

length.notes: No length contrast; stressed syllables are longer than unstressed ones.

intonation.declarative: the lexical pitch patterns of the content words in sequence, with a fall to low at the end of the utterance
intonation.yes_no_question: no change of word order; the end of the utterance is high or rising, and the lexical pattern of the last word is adjusted to it
intonation.wh_question: question word first, fall to the end
intonation.continuation: high or rising end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: set by the tone class of the word: peak on the stressed syllable in the high-low class, peak on the final syllable after a low stressed syllable in the low-high class
intonation.notes: Remijsen and van Heuven (2005) show that the realisation of the word patterns depends on sentence type and on focus. The entries on questions and continuation are general statements and should be read as low confidence.

inventory.name: high-low word pattern (tone class I)
inventory.description: high pitch on the stressed penultimate syllable and low pitch on the final syllable, one digit per syllable; the pattern of nouns, adjectives and most other words of two syllables (para 'bird', biaha 'trip')

inventory.name: low-high word pattern (tone class II)
inventory.description: low pitch on the stressed penultimate syllable and high pitch on the unstressed final syllable, one digit per syllable; the pattern of most verbs of two syllables (para 'to stop', biaha 'to travel') and of some other words
inventory.duration: stressed syllable longer although it is low

inventory.name: final-stress pattern
inventory.description: low unstressed syllables followed by a high stressed final syllable, one digit per syllable; past participles and longer verbs (pará, kantá, kuminsá). It differs from the low-high class in the place of stress, that is in duration and intensity, not in pitch

sandhi: tonal polarisation: unstressed function words and particles take the pitch opposite to that of the neighbouring syllable (Römer 1977, 1991)
tone.neutral_tone: unstressed function words have no fixed tone of their own and are low or polar
tone.notes: The literature agrees that Papiamentu has both contrastive stress and contrastive tone (Römer 1991; Kouwenberg and Murray 1994). Two level tones, high and low, are assumed, and the contrast is clearest in words of two syllables. Tone has a grammatical role: it separates most two-syllable verbs from nouns (Kouwenberg 2004). Remijsen and van Heuven (2005) confirm by measurement that stress and tone are separate, and analyse the contrast as one between words with and without a lexical tone. The Chao digits are schematic, since no published pitch values are cited here. eSpeak NG marks no tone for Papiamento.

problems: no tone at all: the language is set up with the Spanish-type stress settings and the generic intonation, so para 'bird' and para 'to stop', biaha noun and verb, sound the same; only the place of stress is modelled
telling the two tone classes apart needs the part of speech or a word list, since the spelling does not mark tone; the word list has about 120 lines and no tone information
there is no language-specific phoneme table: the generic table base2 is used and schwa is missing, so final -er, -el, -en have a full vowel (hòmber [hˈɔmber])
i and u before a vowel are always glides, which shifts the stress in words such as dia ([djˈa] instead of [ˈdia])
no tune set is selected, so the generic default tunes are used
good: the vowels of the Curaçao spelling are distinguished: è [ɛ], ò [ɔ], ù [ø], ü [y]
the default stress rule (penultimate when the word ends in a vowel, otherwise final) and the acute accent for final stress (kantá, kuminsá) follow the spelling rules
dj, zj, sh, ch, ñ are read as single consonants

notes: The voice is marked as testing. The rules mix the Curaçao spelling with some values of the Aruban and Dutch-based spellings (c, qu, oe, ij). A tone model would need the two-syllable verb class to be marked in the dictionary.
